source: Alfieri, Nokes, Schunn (2011 SREE abstract of the 2013 meta-analysis) Aligning the structural components across learning tasks of case comparisons
finding: Early report of the case-comparison meta-analysis gives d = .60, not .50. The published 2013 Educational Psychologist abstract is reported (search snippet only, not opened) as d = .50 on the same 57 experiments and 336 tests.
numbers: Random effects, 57 experiments (336 tests): d = .60, 95% CI [.47, .72]. Heterogeneous: Q(56) = 136.74, p < .001, I2 = 59.05%.
limits: The .60 is from a 2011 conference abstract before final coding. The .50 figure for the final paper was not read in full text (publisher page 403, Pitt PDF link returned HTML). Cite as 'medium, about .5 to .6'. Human learners, not LLMs.
agent_relevance: Closes gap 5 only partly. Comparison of two cases has a medium human effect; plan an LLM test with two aligned sources, do not quote a single d.

source: Puranam, Sen, Workiewicz (2025) quoting Gick and Holyoak (1983) Experiment 2
finding: A 2025 paper that reran the Gick and Holyoak design reports the original Experiment 2 rates: 29% solved the radiation problem unaided and 50% after a hint.
numbers: Original 1983 Exp 2: 8 of 28 (29%) without hint, 14 of 28 (50%) with hint. 2025 human sample n = 199: factory problem 6.3% without hint, 8.7% (4 of 46) with hint; HR problem 20.3% without hint, 37% (17 of 46) with hint.
quote: 29% ... without a hint and 50% (14 out of 28) with a hint
limits: Secondary quote of the 1983 numbers. The 1980 paper (Exp 1 to 4) could not be opened: the Elsevier page only redirected. 1980 numbers remain unread.
agent_relevance: Spontaneous use of a stored solved case is low and a cue lifts it. Keep an explicit 'check the case store' step in O7 rather than hoping the agent recalls it.

source: Yasunaga et al. (2024) Large language models as analogical reasoners, Table 5 and Section 6.5
finding: With GPT-3.5-turbo, self-generating one exemplar is worse than several. Gains level off at 3 to 5 exemplars. This is the only direct LLM data on 'one source versus several'.
numbers: GSM8K / MATH accuracy by K self-generated exemplars: K=1 76.1 / 34.8; K=2 77.0 / 36.7; K=3 77.5 / 37.3; K=4 77.3 / 37.0; K=5 77.8 / 37.1.
quote: When K = 1, the LLM underperforms due to excessive reliance on a single exemplar generated.
limits: The exemplars are unaligned, self-made, and not comparison-prompted. Gaps are 1 to 3 points. One model. The table layout was garbled in extraction, so the K-to-value order is the most likely reading. It does not test the Gentner 2003 effect (explicit comparison of two cases).
agent_relevance: Weak, indirect support for retrieving 3 sources, not 1. Gap 3 stays open: no test where the agent must compare two aligned sources before transfer.

source: Yasunaga et al. (2024) manual error analysis of 100 GSM8K and MATH problems (Section 6.6)
finding: The closest direct count of how often a carried-over source is wrong. Of 100 hand-checked problems, some self-generated sources had wrong solutions, and wrong or ill-fitting sources went with failures.
numbers: 50 correct answers: 6 irrelevant exemplars, 9 relevant but with incorrect solutions, 35 relevant and correct. 50 wrong answers: 10 irrelevant, 12 relevant but incorrect, 28 relevant and correct but the model still failed (12 generalisation gap, 8 over-reliance on a specific exemplar, 8 other).
limits: GPT-3.5-turbo only. Counts exemplar correctness, not the correctness of individual transferred steps. 100 problems. No test-before-adopt arm.
agent_relevance: Gap 1 partly answered: in this setup 21 of 100 runs carried a source with a wrong solution, and 8 of 50 failures were over-reliance on the source. Supports logging 'candidate failed test' as a metric. A test-before-adopt arm is still unmeasured.

source: Yasunaga et al. (2024) Section 6.4 and Table 4: effect of model scale
finding: Self-generated exemplars help more as the base model gets stronger. For small models, retrieved real exemplars win. For text-davinci-002 and -003 the self-generated version wins.
numbers: Table 4 (GSM8K) rows are garbled in text extraction, so only the direction is recorded: 0-shot CoT < fixed 5-shot CoT < 5-shot retrieved CoT at small scale, and self-generated passes retrieved at the larger scales.
limits: Model scale axis stops at GPT-3 era models. Table values not read cleanly.
agent_relevance: Source recall quality grows with model strength, so a modern agent can self-generate sources. The cost is wrong sources, so keep the test step.

source: Qin et al. (2025) Relevant or Random, Tables 4 and 5: accuracy of self-generated MATH examples
finding: Confirms the dataset label: the example-accuracy table is on MATH. Self-generated 'relevant' examples are less often correct than irrelevant ones.
numbers: Manual check of 50 generated examples per type on MATH (GPT-3.5): relevant 62.0% correct, N/A (no instruction) 72.0%, random same-type 86.0%. Average cosine relevance to the query on GSM8K / MATH: relevant 0.54 / 0.41, random-same 0.30 / 0.20, random-bio 0.06 / 0.11, oracle retrieval 0.65 / 0.63.
quote: while the examples generated by 'relevant' are more related to the test query, they are less accurate
limits: n = 50 per type, single check. Correct-but-irrelevant examples win only on math. On BBH relevance helped (see d07).
agent_relevance: Resolves the c13 label doubt. Relevant sources are harder, so more often wrong. Test sources for correctness, not only similarity.

source: Qin et al. (2025) Tables 1, 2, 15 and A.8: other tasks and stronger models
finding: The accuracy-over-relevance finding is task-dependent. On BBH relevant examples win. On two math sets and with GPT-4o-mini and Llama models they lose to irrelevant ones. No reasoning model was tested.
numbers: BBH average (5 tasks, GPT-3.5): relevant 63.2, random-same 61.9, random-bio 60.4. GSM8K+MATH average: N/A 55.8, random-same 55.7, random-bio 54.9. GPT-4o-mini GSM8K: relevant 90.7, N/A 91.9, random-same 92.6, random-diff 92.3, random-bio 93.2, ICL-math 94.2, ICL-bio 94.5. Irrelevant beats relevant also at k = 3 (A.8). Llama-2-70b, Llama-3-8B, Llama-3.1-8B also reported.
limits: Largest model is GPT-4o-mini. Gains are 1 to 3 points. No o1/o3 class or frontier model, no non-math task other than BBH. Gap 4 stays open for frontier models.
agent_relevance: Gap 4 partly closed: holds for GPT-4o-mini and Llama on GSM8K, fails on BBH. Rule for the agent: verify the source's answer, do not rank sources by similarity alone.

source: Yu, He, Ying (2024) Thought Propagation, Table 1 (shortest path) and layer study
finding: Solving analogous problems and aggregating their solutions into the target beats direct prompting and ToT at about ToT token cost. One-layer TP is near ToT cost; two layers cost more for small gains.
numbers: Optimal rate (OR), 0-shot: GPT-3.5 IO 0.33, CoT 0.26, ToT 0.22, TP 0.65; GPT-4 IO 0.78, CoT 0.76, ToT 0.46, TP 0.88; PaLM-2 IO 0.14, CoT 0.24, TP 0.36. 5-shot GPT-4 TP 0.86 vs ToT 0.77. Over-length rate GPT-4 0-shot TP 0.05 vs IO 0.10. 100 shortest-path problems.
limits: One task family where analogous problems are built by the method itself. No external check of each carried step except the aggregation module. Not independently replicated.
agent_relevance: Gap 2/1 partial: shows transfer plus aggregation beats scratch solving at similar cost, but it is not a test-before-adopt contrast.

source: Sourati et al. (2024) ARN Table 2 (arXiv v4)
finding: Full ARN table read. The far-analogy figure of 39.6 is the mean of two far partitions: far analogy against far distractor 45.3 and against near distractor 33.9 (all-model averages). GPT-4 got 57.1 and 29.1 there. This explains the 57 vs 75 vs 39.6 puzzle in the critique.
numbers: Accuracy %, chance 50: GPT-4 (near,far) 94.0, (near,near) 92.5, (far,far) 57.1, (far,near) 29.1, average 68.1. GPT-3.5 88.1, 81.3, 50.4, 21.7, avg 60.3. All-model average 76.9, 73.2, 45.3, 33.9 = 57.3. Humans 98.6, 97.2, 96.8, 91.4 = 96.0. 548 query-distractor pairs.
quote: models only achieved 39.6% on average (worse than random performance) when solving far analogies
limits: Models are 2023 to 2024 (GPT-4.0, GPT-3.5, Llama-2, Flan-T5). The (far,near) cell can be solved by choosing the dissimilar story, so it is a surface-similarity trap. Few-shot and CoT raised scores but the best model stayed halfway between chance and humans. The 39.6 in the text is described for models overall, not GPT-4 alone; GPT-4's own far mean is (57.1+29.1)/2 = 43.1.
agent_relevance: The failure is choosing structure over surface. A source-selection step should mask surface overlap or check the relations explicitly.

source: McGovern, Craig, Lippincott, Sirin (2026) When models know more than they say, Table 3
finding: On ARN stories recast as ranking (20 candidates), 2026 frontier models do much better than small Llama models. This is a fresh data point for gap 6, though it is not the binary far-analogy test.
numbers: Narrative parallelism ranking, MAP: Claude Opus 4.5 and GPT-5.2 about 0.82 (MRR 0.91). Open models Llama-3.2-1B and Llama-8B instruct about 0.35 (probing of open models also about 0.35).
limits: Different metric from Sourati et al. Far and near cases are not split out, so the GPT-4 collapse on far-with-near-distractor cannot be compared. Preprint under review. Table rows partly garbled in extraction.
agent_relevance: Suggests the far-analogy collapse eased by 2026 on the ranking version, but the hard cell was not isolated. Gap 6 stays open for the far-with-near-distractor cell.

source: Camposampiero et al. (2025) Can large reasoning models do analogical reasoning under perceptual uncertainty?
finding: Reasoning models solve symbolic Raven-style analogies well but fall to near chance when inputs get longer, wider in range and noisy. More reasoning tokens did not fix it.
numbers: I-RAVEN to I-RAVEN-X: o3-mini 86.6% to 17.0% with 3.4 times more reasoning tokens; DeepSeek R1 80.6% to 23.2%. Chance 12.5%. o3-mini high effort: +6% on I-RAVEN, flat on the hard set; up to 31.0% at 53,596 reasoning tokens. Neuro-symbolic ARLC 98.6% to 88.0%.
limits: Raven matrices, not verbal analogy and not candidate inference. Shows reasoning models can be brittle out of distribution.
agent_relevance: Reasoning-trained models are not immune to analogy brittleness (relevant to gaps 6 and 8). A code-side symbolic check held up where free reasoning did not.

source: Khojasteh et al. (2026) YARN: structural mapping with LLM-derived abstractions, Table 3
finding: A greedy one-to-one structure mapping over LLM-abstracted event units beats LLM-only mapping on a 4-way multiple-choice analogy set, and on far ARN for Llama, but not clearly for Qwen. Mapping without abstraction is below chance.
numbers: MCQ (chance 0.25): Qwen3-8B best LLM-only 0.41 (CoT) vs YARN 0.46; Llama-3.1-8B LLM-only 0.28 vs YARN 0.45; unabstracted structural mapping 0.17 (Qwen). ARN far (chance 0.50): Qwen YARN 0.47 vs zero-shot 0.52; Llama YARN 0.46 vs 0.42. ARN near: Qwen CoT 0.79 vs YARN 0.69; Llama zero-shot 0.73 vs YARN 0.76.
limits: 8B open models only. Task is picking the analogous story, not choosing which source steps to carry. No matched-compute report. Table cells garbled in extraction; figures taken from the text paragraph. Far ARN stays below 0.50 in most settings.
agent_relevance: Gap 2 only partly answered: a code-side one-to-one check helps weak models on choice, with mixed results, and it needs good abstraction first. No evidence yet for step selection.

source: Shen, Druckmann, Zou (2026) Unlocking LLM creativity in science through analogical reasoning, human study (App. C.1)
finding: Humans judge analogy-guided solutions as more novel but less often reasonable. This is the only human check of correctness-like quality, and it is not a blind expert correctness test.
numbers: 50 pairs (one analogy-guided, one cross-domain baseline), 4 biomedical AI researchers, 25 pairs each. AR judged more novel 78% of the time (Cohen kappa 0.445). Judged a reasonable approach: AR 67% (kappa 0.155), cross-domain baseline 86% (kappa 0.416).
quote: the increased perceived novelty of the AR solutions may come at a cost of being a less reasonable solution
limits: Four annotators, one random solution per problem, source domain shown to raters so not blind to method. 'Reasonable' means plausible, not verified correct. Authors state feasibility is a bottleneck.
agent_relevance: Gap 10 answered 'no': the novelty gain comes with a 19 point drop in judged reasonableness. A candidate-inference test is needed before adopting far-domain steps.

source: Shen et al. (2026) novelty scores and downstream checks
finding: Analogy-guided generation raises LLM-judged novelty a lot. Downstream code was implemented for four biomedical tasks, which is a partial execution check.
numbers: Stratified novelty (1 to 10), no-domain < cross-domain < AR: Claude 1.28 / 3.12 / 5.54; GPT 1.98 / 3.69 / 6.14; Gemini 2.11 / 4.68 / 6.43. Binary novelty: Claude 1.6% / 21.6% / 50.4%; GPT 8.8% / 27.2% / 58.8%; Gemini 8.6% / 37.9% / 68.8%. 50 problems, 5 solutions each. LLM-judge novelty checked against 98 expert-scored NLP ideas from another dataset. Cost about $0.02 per problem.
limits: Judge is an LLM scored against retrieved literature. Domain is biomedicine. The execution results are four case studies, not a rate of correct steps.
agent_relevance: Novelty is cheap to raise; correctness is the open piece. Keep the test step after any far-domain transfer.

source: Lewis and Mitchell (2025) Evaluating the robustness of analogical reasoning in LLMs, Tables 4 and 5
finding: Re-read for gap 8. GPT-4 is biased toward the first listed answer and drops more than people when the correct story is paraphrased. Only GPT models of the 2023 to 2024 era were tested; no reasoning-trained model.
numbers: 18 far-analogy story problems. Correct answer first vs second: GPT-4 (Webb et al. data) 0.89 (16/18) vs 0.61 (11/18), total 0.75; GPT-4 (their run) 1.0 vs 0.72, total 0.86 (31/36); humans 0.78 (292/373) vs 0.78 (272/347), total 0.78 (564/720). Paraphrased correct story: GPT-4 0.86 to 0.72 (26/36); humans 0.78 to 0.70 (503/720).
limits: 18 stories; the authors say the paraphrase gap is not shown significant. No shuffle-and-vote arm. No o1/o3/R1 test found this session.
agent_relevance: Gap 8 stays open. Cheap defence to build in: shuffle candidate order across runs and vote.

source: Puranam, Sen, Workiewicz (2025) Can LLMs help improve analogical reasoning, with-hint and no-hint matching
finding: With two stories (one right, one wrong) GPT-4 either misses the analogy or over-uses it. With a hint it always applies an analogy, and about half the time the wrong one.
numbers: GPT-4 (Sept 2024), n = 60 (15 per cell). No hint: Radiation story used 1 of 15 (6.7%), recall 0, precision 0, accuracy 50%. With hint: recall 1.00, precision 0.50 to 0.52, F1 0.67 to 0.68, accuracy 50 to 53%. Humans with hint: precision 0.67 to 0.75, recall 0.26 to 0.39, accuracy 57 to 63%.
limits: One model, small cells, business-case problems. Authors flag a possible demand effect.
agent_relevance: Best direct count so far of wrong-source application by an LLM (about 50% when cued). Supports a source-check step before transfer; it is a proxy for gap 1, not a measure of step falseness.

source: Ye, Wang, Khashabi (2024) AnaloBench, Table 7 appendix
finding: Picking the analogous story among 4 collapses with story length. Scale helps on one-sentence stories but not on long ones.
numbers: T1 accuracy at 1 / 10 / 30 sentences (chance 25%): GPT-3.5 71.8 / 51.2 / 31.5; XwinLM-70B 55.6 / 39.2 / 29.5; LLaMA2-70B 35.6 / 26.5 / 26.3; Tulu2-70B 50.0 / 25.0 / 27.9. Authors: no model beat humans in any setting; performance plateaus with size on long stories.
limits: 2023 to 2024 models. The GPT-4 row did not extract cleanly so it is not recorded.
agent_relevance: Real source cases are long. Compress each source into a short relational summary before matching.

source: Gap note: direct measures not found this session
finding: Search quota ran out (WebSearch refused; arXiv and Semantic Scholar APIs returned 429 on many tries; OpenAlex needed a key). No paper was found that (a) counts false carried steps with and without a test, (b) compares one vs two aligned sources for LLMs, (c) probes skolem-style missing-entity repair, (d) tests order or paraphrase robustness in reasoning models, (e) gives Lassaline or Spellman and Holyoak numbers.
numbers: Not applicable. Papers opened: ARN, Qin, Yasunaga, Thought Propagation, YARN, Shen, McGovern, Camposampiero, AnaloBench, Puranam, Lewis and Mitchell.
limits: Absence is for this session's reachable corpus, not proof that none exist. The Lassaline PsycNet page did not load.
agent_relevance: Treat gaps 1, 3, 7, 8, 9 as open and run them as our own bench arms (O7 with and without the test step; one vs two sources).
